meta.topic: AI vs ML vs Deep Learning
meta.title: AI vs ML vs Deep Learning
meta.thesis: AI, machine learning, and deep learning are three nested circles — deep learning inside ML inside AI — and knowing which one you have tells you its data needs, cost, and how explainable it can be.

modules.title: The nested picture: AI, ML, deep learning
modules.sub: Starts the spine: why these three terms exist and how they nest.
modules.summary: AI is the broad goal of making machines do smart things; machine learning is the subset that learns from data; deep learning is the subset of ML that uses many-layered neural networks. They are nested circles, not three competing things.
objectives: Explain why AI, ML, and deep learning are nested rather than rival categories.
State the one defining trait of each in plain language.
Catch the most common confusion: treating 'AI' and 'deep learning' as synonyms.

spans.text: Why this distinction exists:

every product now claims to use "AI." That word covers everything from a hand-written if/else rule to a billion-parameter network. If you can place a system in the right circle, you instantly know what data it needs, how it can fail, and whether you can explain its answers.
Before reading on, predict:
is every machine-learning system also an AI system? And is every AI system also machine learning?

blocks.title: Three nested circles, not three rivals
blocks.analogy: Think of Russian nesting dolls: deep learning sits inside machine learning, which sits inside AI. Opening the big doll never removes the small ones.

spans.text: The single most useful picture of
AI vs ML vs Deep Learning
is three circles, one inside the next.

items.text: ai
(the outer circle) — any technique that makes a machine do something we associate with human intelligence, including plain hand-written rules.
ml
(inside AI) — the subset where the machine learns the rules from
data
instead of being told them.
Deep learning
(inside ML) — the subset of ML that uses many-layered neural networks to learn features straight from raw input.

spans.text: So every deep-learning system is machine learning, and every machine-learning system is AI — but not the reverse. A thermostat rule is AI but not ML; spam filtering with hand-picked features is ML but not deep learning.

blocks.title: Zoom from the outer circle to the inner one
blocks.caption: Slide inward to see how each circle narrows the definition — broad goal, then learning-from-data, then neural networks.

stops.label: AI (outer)
stops.note: Any machine behavior that looks intelligent. A chess program with hand-coded rules counts. No learning required.

stops.label: Machine learning (middle)
stops.note: Now the rules are learned from examples. You still choose which features matter — e.g. word counts for spam.

stops.label: Deep learning (inner)
stops.note: A many-layered neural network learns the features itself from raw pixels, audio, or text. Most data-hungry, least transparent.

blocks.title: Place any system in the right circle

steps.label: Ask: does it learn from data?

spans.text: If a human wrote every rule by hand, it is
ai
but not machine learning. If it improves from examples, it is ML.
If you fed it hand-chosen signals (word counts, pixel averages), it is classic
ml
. If a neural network learned the features from raw input, it is deep learning.
"This is AI, specifically ML, specifically deep learning" — or stop at the first circle that fits. The narrowest true label tells you the most.
The same task — flagging spam email — can live in any of the three circles:

items.text: Rule-based AI:
a human writes "if subject contains 'FREE MONEY', flag it." No learning. AI, not ML.
Classic ML:
you count chosen words per email and train a
model
to weigh them. ML, not deep learning.
Deep learning:
a neural network reads the raw email text and learns its own signals. Most powerful, most data-hungry, hardest to explain.

spans.text: Same goal, three very different answers to "how much data, how explainable, how expensive."
Technically, the boundaries are about where the function comes from. Rule-based AI: a human encodes the function f(x). Classic
ml
: an algorithm fits f(x) to data using human-engineered features. Deep learning: a network learns both the features and f(x) end-to-end.
The litmus test: if removing the training data would leave the system unable to function, it is machine learning — not just rule-based AI.

blocks.prompt: A thermostat that turns on heat when the temperature drops below a hand-set rule — which circle is it in?

options.text: Deep learning, because it reacts to its environment.
AI but not machine learning, because the rule was written by a human, not learned from data.
Machine learning, because it makes a decision.

blocks.explanation: Making a decision is not the same as learning. The thermostat follows a human-written rule, so it sits in the AI circle but outside the ML circle.

modules.title: How each one actually learns
modules.sub: Follows the nested picture: now open up the mechanism inside each circle.
modules.summary: The circles differ in who supplies the logic. Rule-based AI gets it from a human. Classic ML learns it from data using features a human chose. Deep learning learns the features and the logic together. The shared engine of both ML kinds is: minimize a loss, then check that it generalizes.
objectives: Describe the shared ML training loop: predict, measure loss, adjust, repeat.
Explain what deep learning adds: learning features from raw data automatically.
Distinguish fitting the training data from generalizing to new data.

blocks.title: The training loop hiding inside ML
blocks.analogy: Learning from data is like tuning a guitar by ear: play a note, hear how far off it is (the loss), adjust the peg, repeat until it sounds right on songs you have not played yet.

spans.text: Both classic
ml
and deep learning run the same basic loop to build a
model

items.text: Predict on a training example with the current settings.
Measure how wrong it was — the
loss
Adjust the settings a little to reduce that loss.
Repeat over many examples until the loss stops falling.

spans.text: The difference is what gets adjusted. Classic ML adjusts weights over features
you
chose. Deep learning stacks many layers and adjusts them all, so the network discovers useful features from raw input by itself.
The
model
begins with random settings and predicts a label for one example — usually badly.
The
loss
function turns 'how wrong' into a single number the algorithm can shrink.

steps.label: Nudge and re-check on new data

spans.text: After many nudges, hold out data the model never trained on and confirm it still scores well — that is
generalization
, the only success that counts.
Goal: predict a house's price.

items.text: Classic ML:
you hand it the features that matter — square footage, bedrooms, zip code — and it learns a weight for each. You can read the weights and explain the prediction.
Deep learning:
you could feed it raw listing photos and text, and it learns its own internal features ("granite counters," "good light"). More powerful, but you cannot easily say why it priced one house high.

spans.text: Both shrink a
loss
; only the deep model invents its own features.
Before deep learning, the hard part of
ml

was feature engineering — humans hand-crafting the inputs. Deep networks replaced that with representation learning: each layer composes the previous layer's outputs into higher-level features, so raw pixels become edges, then shapes, then objects, with no human in the loop.
Rule of thumb: deep learning trades human feature work for far more data and compute. On small, tabular problems that trade rarely pays off.

blocks.prompt: What is the main thing deep learning adds on top of classic machine learning?

options.text: It removes the need for any training data.
It learns the features from raw input itself, instead of using human-chosen features.
It is always more accurate than classic ML on every problem.

blocks.explanation: Deep learning's signature move is representation learning: the network discovers useful features from raw data, where classic ML relies on features a human selected. It still needs data, and it is not universally more accurate.

modules.title: Choosing: classic ML or deep learning?
modules.sub: Follows the mechanism: now use it to make the one choice that matters.
modules.summary: Knowing the circles is only useful if it changes what you build. The real decision is rarely 'AI or not' — it is 'classic ML or deep learning', and it turns on how much labeled data you have, whether you must explain the answer, and what compute you can afford. The default should be the simplest model that meets the need.
objectives: Pick between rule-based AI, classic ML, and deep learning for a given problem.
Weigh data volume, interpretability, and cost against each other.
Justify defaulting to the simplest approach that solves the problem.

blocks.title: The default should be the simplest thing that works

spans.text: It is tempting to reach for deep learning because it is the most powerful circle. But power you do not need is cost you do not need: more labeled data, more compute, and far less ability to explain the answer.
Three questions settle most choices:

items.text: How much labeled data do you have?
Deep learning is hungry; thousands-plus examples before it earns its keep.
Must you explain the decision?
Regulated or high-stakes calls favor an interpretable
model
What can you afford to run?
A linear model runs on a laptop; a deep network may need GPUs.

spans.text: If a handful of hand-written rules solve it, you are done — that is
ai
with no training data to collect and nothing to retrain.
If patterns are too messy for rules but your data is tabular and modest, a classic
ml
model is usually faster to ship and easier to debug.

steps.label: Escalate to deep learning only when needed

spans.text: Raw images, audio, or language at scale — and enough labeled data — is where deep learning's
generalization
advantage finally pays for its cost.

blocks.title: Rule-based AI vs classic ML vs deep learning

options.name: Rule-based AI

cells.text: None to train — a human writes the logic.
Fully transparent; you can read every rule.
Stable problems with a few clear conditions.

options.whenToUse: Use when a handful of rules already capture the logic.

options.name: Classic ML

cells.text: Modest, often tabular, with chosen features.
Often readable; you can inspect feature weights.

options.whenToUse: Use when rules fail but data is modest and you want explainability.

options.name: Deep learning

cells.text: Large labeled sets, often raw and unstructured.
Hard to explain why it decided what it did.

options.whenToUse: Use when input is raw perception data and you have lots of it.

blocks.howToRead: Move down the list and stop at the first option that meets the requirement. Pick deep learning only when the data type and volume actually demand it.

spans.text: Deep learning's accuracy is not free: it shifts work to data labeling, compute, and tuning, and it makes failures harder to diagnose because the learned features are opaque. A classic
ml
model that is 2% less accurate but fully explainable is often the better production choice.
Ship the simplest model that clears the bar, then escalate only when measured performance demands it.

blocks.prompt: You have 300 rows of tabular customer data and must explain every decision to an auditor. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Deep learning, because it is the most accurate option available.
Classic ML, because the data is small and tabular and the model stays explainable.
Whatever has the most parameters, since bigger is always better.

blocks.explanation: With little data and a hard interpretability requirement, deep learning is the wrong tool. A classic ML model trains on modest tabular data and lets you show the auditor which features drove the decision.

modules.decisionItForces: Pick the narrowest circle that solves the problem: rule-based AI, classic ML, or deep learning.

modules.title: A tiny machine-learning model, for real
modules.sub: Follows the choice: make it concrete by training a real classic-ML model.
modules.summary: Eight lines train an actual machine-learning model: split the data, fit a classifier, and score it on data it never saw. This is classic ML — not deep learning — and it makes the training loop from module 2 something you can run.
objectives: Read a minimal scikit-learn training script end to end.
Identify which line does the learning and which line measures generalization.
Verify an AI-generated ML snippet before you trust its score.

blocks.title: What 'training a model' looks like in code

spans.text: The training loop from module 2 is only a few lines in practice. You split your data so you can test honestly, fit a
model
on the training half, and then score it on the half it never saw.
That last step is the whole point: a high score on data the model already memorized proves nothing. A high score on held-out data is
generalization

blocks.title: Read the script in three moves

spans.text: Hold back part of the data as a test set so the score later means something.
The
model
learns weights from the training half — this single call is the learning.
Evaluate on the held-out half to estimate
generalization
to new data.

blocks.title: This is ML, not deep learning

spans.text: The model below is logistic regression — a classic
ml
algorithm with no neural-network layers. It is squarely inside the ML circle and outside the deep-learning circle.
If you swapped it for a multi-layer neural net on the same tiny dataset, you would add complexity and risk overfitting without gaining accuracy. The right circle here is the smaller one.

blocks.title: Train and score a classic ML model in 8 lines
blocks.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=0)
model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=200).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print(model.score(Xte, yte))  # accuracy on data it never trained on

spans.text: Three flowers, four measurements each. The model learns to map measurements to species, then reports accuracy on the held-out test set — a real, if tiny,
generalization
check.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Before reading on, predict: which single line does the actual learning, and which line would a beginner mistakenly use to judge the model?
predictThenReveal.answer: The .fit(Xtr, ytr) call does the learning. The trap is judging the model by its score on Xtr (the training data); the honest number is model.score(Xte, yte) on held-out data.

syntax.explains: Holds back part of the data so the score is honest, not memorized.
A classic ML model — linear, no neural-network layers.
Runs the training loop: this is where learning happens.
Measures generalization on data the model never saw.

spans.text: Verify before you trust an AI-generated ML snippet.
Assistants often produce code that looks right but reports a misleading score. Check these four things:

items.text: Is the score computed on a held-out test set, not on the training data? Scoring on Xtr inflates accuracy.
Is there a real train/test split before fitting? No split means no honest
generalization
number.
Does the model converge? A warning about max_iter means the reported accuracy may be wrong.
Is the chosen
model
appropriate for the data size — classic ML for small/tabular, not an oversized network?

blocks.prompt: In the eight-line script, which line tells you whether the model actually learned anything useful?

options.text: The import lines, because they load the algorithm.
model.score(Xte, yte), because it measures accuracy on data the model never trained on.
load_iris, because it provides the data.

blocks.explanation: Learning is only proven by performance on unseen data. The score on the held-out test set (Xte, yte) is the generalization check; everything before it just sets up the experiment.

modules.title: Where it breaks — then check yourself
modules.sub: Closes the spine: the traps that bite beginners, then active recall.
modules.summary: The most common mistakes are not technical — they are conceptual: calling everything 'AI', assuming deep learning is always best, and trusting a model that memorized its training data. Spot these, recall the core ideas from memory, and the distinction is yours.
objectives: Name the three confusions that most often trip up beginners.
Recognize overfitting as a failure to generalize, not a bug in the code.
Recall the nested picture and the training loop without looking back.

spans.text: Before reading on, predict from memory:
back in module 2 you met the training loop. What single number does an ML model try to shrink, and what does a good score on held-out data prove?
(The answer: it shrinks the
loss
, and a good score on unseen data proves
generalization
— that it learned the pattern, not the examples.)
These are the misreadings that cause real mistakes — in conversations, in tool choices, and in budgets.
1. Calling everything "AI"
A hand-coded rule and a billion-parameter network are both
ai
, but they need wildly different data, cost, and oversight. Flattening them hides which one you actually have.
2. Assuming deep learning is always best
On small, tabular, or interpretability-critical problems, a classic
ml
model often wins on speed, cost, and explainability. Bigger is not automatically better.
3. Overfitting: trusting a memorizer (non-obvious)
A
model
can score nearly perfectly on its training data and still fail on new data. That is overfitting — a failure of
generalization
, not a crash. It is invisible unless you test on held-out data.
First diagnostic: if someone quotes a model's accuracy without saying it was measured on held-out data, treat the number as unproven.

blocks.prompt: A teammate says their model is 99% accurate — but only on the data it was trained on. What is the most likely problem?

options.text: Nothing — high accuracy is always good news.
Overfitting: the model may have memorized the training data and could fail to generalize to new data.
The model is too small and needs more layers.

blocks.explanation: Accuracy on training data tells you almost nothing. A model can memorize its examples and still fail on anything new — that is overfitting, a failure of generalization. The honest test is held-out data.

finalCheck.title: Knowledge check
finalCheck.intro: A quick check across the whole lesson — pick or type your answers.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the relationship between AI, ML, and deep learning?

options.text: They are three different names for the same technology.
Deep learning and ML are rivals that compete to solve the same problems.
ML is a subset of AI, and deep learning is a subset of ML — like nested circles.
AI is the newest of the three and contains the other two.

questions.explanation: The three form a nesting: every ML system is an AI system, and every deep learning system is an ML system — they are not rivals or synonyms.

questions.prompt: In the standard ML training loop, what happens immediately after the model makes a prediction?

options.text: The model is deployed to production.
The loss (error) is measured by comparing the prediction to the correct answer.
New training data is collected to replace the old data.
The features are automatically extracted from raw input.

questions.explanation: The loop is: predict → measure loss → adjust weights → repeat. Measuring the loss is the step that tells the model how wrong it was.

questions.prompt: A small startup has a structured spreadsheet of 800 customer records and needs to predict churn. They have no GPU budget and need results their manager can explain. Which approach fits best?

options.text: A large deep learning model, because it learns features automatically.
A classic ML model (e.g., logistic regression or a decision tree), because it matches the data size and interpretability need.
A hand-written rule-based system, because no data-driven approach is needed.
Deep learning with a pre-trained model, because transfer learning removes the data requirement.

questions.explanation: Classic ML is the narrowest circle that solves the problem here: small structured data, low compute budget, and a need for interpretability all point away from deep learning.

questions.prompt:
Look at this two-line scikit-learn snippet:

```python
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
score = model.score(X_test, y_test)
```

Which line does the *learning*, and which line measures *generalization*? Explain in one sentence each.
questions.acceptableAnswer: model.fit(X_train, y_train) is where learning happens — it adjusts the model's parameters using the training data. model.score(X_test, y_test) measures generalization — it checks how well the model performs on data it has never seen before.
questions.explanation: fit() is the training step; score() on held-out test data is the generalization check. Using test data the model never trained on is what makes the score meaningful.

questions.prompt: A model scores 99% accuracy on its training data but only 61% on new data. What is the most likely problem?

options.text: There is a bug in the training code that inflates the score.
The model has overfit — it memorized the training data instead of learning patterns that generalize.
The test dataset is too large and is confusing the model.
Deep learning was used when classic ML should have been chosen.

questions.explanation: Overfitting means the model learned the training data too specifically — it performs well in-sample but fails on unseen data. It is a generalization failure, not a code bug.
